titulo: Module 10 — Exam: context management and prompt caching

questoes.pergunta: A retailer runs a support agent on the Agent SDK. The get_order tool returns the complete order object (about 40 fields, including logistics history), and the agent only uses status, amount, date, and items. In long conversations, the agent starts mixing up values, and the cost per support interaction has risen sharply. What is the BEST first action?
opcoes: Migrate to a model with a larger context window
Add to the system prompt the instruction "ignore the irrelevant order fields"
Make the tool (or a PostToolUse hook) return only the fields relevant to the support interaction
Enable compaction with a low threshold to summarize the get_order results as soon as they are no longer needed
questoes.explicacao: Tool output is the biggest silent consumer of context. Cutting it at the source reduces cost per turn and attention noise, and it is the simplest fix that solves the problem.
feedbacks: Tempting because it seems to "give more room", but it makes each turn more expensive and doesn't reduce the noise; it attacks the symptom.
The tokens still come in and are still paid for; asking the model to ignore them is probabilistic and doesn't reduce cost.
Correct. Return only what the agent uses.
Compaction would summarize values that need to be exact (risk of losing numbers) and is more complex than simply not bringing in the junk.

questoes.pergunta: In a support agent, after about 40 turns the history is summarized automatically. The team noticed that, after the summary, the agent sometimes calls process_refund with a rounded amount or with the order_id of another order mentioned in the conversation. What is the correct design?
opcoes: Keep a case facts block (IDs, amounts, dates) outside the summary, reinjected on every turn
Rewrite the summarization prompt asking it to preserve numbers and IDs exactly
Increase the number of turns before the summary to 80
Add a second model that compares the summary with the original history and corrects divergent numbers and IDs
questoes.explicacao: Summaries lose exact values and IDs. Whatever becomes a tool argument can't be paraphrased: it goes in a case facts block that is never summarized.
feedbacks: Correct. Transactional facts stay out of the summary's reach.
Tempting, but summarization remains probabilistic; it will still lose or round values sometimes.
Only postpones the problem and increases cost and lost in the middle.
A more complex solution than necessary (another model checking the first) and still probabilistic.

questoes.pergunta: A multi-agent research system combines the reports of 6 subagents into a single 120,000-token context before asking the synthesizer for conclusions. The findings of the regulatory subagent, which sit in the middle of the concatenation, are frequently omitted from the synthesis. Which adjustment is most appropriate?
opcoes: Increase the synthesizer's max_tokens
Ask the subagents for structured summaries and put the key findings at the beginning, with per-source headers
Shuffle the order of the reports randomly on each run
Use a model with a 1M-token window so the 120,000 tokens take up a small fraction of the context
questoes.explicacao: Lost in the middle: the middle of long contexts receives less attention. Key findings at the beginning, with section headers, and less raw volume.
feedbacks: max_tokens limits the output; the problem is attention to the input.
Correct. Reduces volume, positions the critical content, and structures it with headers.
Randomizing only changes what gets ignored; it doesn't solve the problem.
More room doesn't improve attention to the middle; it tends to make it worse.

questoes.pergunta: A developer uses Claude Code in a long refactoring session. At the start, they explained that "the integration tests need the ORDERS_DB_URL variable pointing to the test container". After a /compact, Claude started running the tests against the default configuration. What is the best way to prevent this from now on?
opcoes: Avoid /compact and let the session grow to the limit
Repeat the instruction every 10 messages
Run /compact more often, so the summary is generated while the instruction is still recent in the conversation
Record the convention in the project's CLAUDE.md, which is reloaded and survives /compact
questoes.explicacao: What must not be lost goes into a file. CLAUDE.md survives /compact; older details from the conversation can be lost.
feedbacks: The session degrades, and sooner or later it will compact or overflow anyway.
Depends on manual discipline and pollutes the context; it isn't a design.
Compacting more often loses more details, not fewer.
Correct. A permanent instruction goes into a file that is loaded in every session.

questoes.pergunta: A team uses Claude Code to understand a 2-million-line .NET monolith. After dozens of greps and reads, the main session's answers have become generic ("the module follows typical repository patterns") and it rereads files it has already analyzed. Which change of approach is most effective?
opcoes: Delegate the exploration to subagents (e.g., Explore) that return only a summary of the findings
Ask Claude to read all of the module's files at once at the start, to have the complete context before answering
Increase effort to max
Restart the session from scratch whenever the answers become vague, without saving anything
questoes.explicacao: The exploration noise stays in the subagent's context; the main session receives only the conclusion. It's the classic mitigation for a large codebase.
feedbacks: Correct. A subagent isolates the noise and returns a summary.
Reading everything up front is the anti-pattern that exhausts the context.
More effort doesn't restore attention to a saturated context.
Loses all the findings; with no saved state, it starts over from scratch.

questoes.pergunta: A research coordinator delegates 8 sequential subtasks that take hours. In the last run, the process crashed after completing 3 of them, and the new run redid everything from the beginning. Which mechanism solves this?
opcoes: Resume the previous session with --resume and rely on the history to know which subtasks were already completed
Reduce the number of subtasks to fit in a single window
Keep a manifest in a known location (tasks, status, partial results) that is read at startup
Increase the coordinator's max_tokens
questoes.explicacao: State saved in a known location + a manifest lets the new run read what was already completed and resume from there.
feedbacks: Tempting, but the session may have crashed in the middle of a step, and the history isn't a reliable record of state; the state needs to live outside the conversation.
Changes the problem instead of solving it; long-running work is still subject to failures.
Correct. A manifest is the basis for resuming after a crash.
Has nothing to do with state persistence.

questoes.pergunta: In a long Claude Code session investigating a concurrency bug, Claude started forgetting hypotheses that had already been ruled out and proposing them again. Which TWO measures directly address the problem? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Increase --max-turns
Ask Claude to record hypotheses, evidence, and ruled-out items in a draft file (scratchpad) and consult it
Switch the permission mode to acceptEdits
Disable CLAUDE.md to free up space
Run /compact proactively, with an instruction to focus on the ruled-out hypotheses and the evidence, before the session degrades further
questoes.explicacao: A scratchpad survives compression and keeps the findings; a proactive, focused /compact reduces noise while preserving what's essential.
feedbacks: The number of turns has nothing to do with remembering findings.
Correct. A draft file persists outside the scrollback.
The permission mode doesn't affect context.
CLAUDE.md is small and useful; removing it takes away project context without solving the forgetting.
Correct. Compacting before degradation sets in, with a focus, is a recommended mitigation.

questoes.pergunta: A research agent makes about 200 web search calls per task, each result with ~3,000 tokens. The older results have already been incorporated into the agent's own synthesis notes, but they still take up the window. What is the BEST option?
opcoes: Use the memory tool to move the old results to files and reduce what stays in the window
Use context editing to clear old tool results that have already been consumed
Use a case facts block with the results
Reduce to 50 searches per task
questoes.explicacao: Context editing (clearing old tool results) was built for verbose agentic loops whose old content has already been used.
feedbacks: The memory tool is for persisting across sessions; it isn't the mechanism for trimming the current session.
Correct.
Case facts is for a few exact values; putting search results there would increase the context.
Limits the quality of the research without addressing the buildup of already-consumed results.

questoes.pergunta: A team enabled server-side compaction in a long-running C# agent. Even so, the requests grow until they hit the limit. The loop does: history.Add(new Message("assistant", response.Content[0].Text)). What should be fixed?
opcoes: Lower the compaction trigger threshold
Add a cache breakpoint on the last block
Replace compaction with context editing, which doesn't depend on the response format to work
Append the entire response.Content to the history, preserving the compaction block
questoes.explicacao: The response includes a compaction block. Appending only the text silently discards that state, and the compaction never takes effect.
feedbacks: The compaction block is still discarded; the threshold doesn't matter.
Caching doesn't reduce the size of the history.
Switches mechanisms without fixing the bug; and the code would still lose tool_use/thinking blocks.
Correct. Append the entire content, not just the text.

questoes.pergunta: To comply with LGPD, a team decided that, on every turn, it would walk through the history already sent and replace CPFs with "***" in older messages before the next request. After that, 400 errors started appearing on models with thinking, and the cache stopped getting reads. What is the correct approach?
opcoes: Mask the CPF before it enters the history (PostToolUse or in the tool) and keep the history append-only
Turn off thinking so the history can be edited freely, and keep replacing the CPFs on every turn
Move the editing to the system prompt
Increase the cache TTL to 1 hour
questoes.explicacao: Editing old turns breaks preserved thinking blocks (400) and invalidates the cache prefix. Sensitive data should be handled at the input, keeping the history append-only.
feedbacks: Correct. Clean it at the source; never rewrite the past.
Attacks the symptom, sacrifices quality, and still invalidates the cache.
Doesn't solve it: the CPF remains in the old messages.
TTL doesn't help when the prefix changes.

questoes.pergunta: A support agent serves the same customer several times a month. The company wants agreements made in one interaction (e.g., "customer prefers contact by email; 20 BRL credit promised") to be available in the next one, days later. Which mechanism should be used?
opcoes: Compaction with a high threshold
Context editing that preserves the last interaction and clears the earlier ones, to keep the recent agreements in the window
Persistent memory (memory tool) with per-customer findings, read at the start of the next interaction
Prompt caching with a 1-hour TTL
questoes.explicacao: Findings that need to hold across sessions go into persistent memory outside the conversation.
feedbacks: Compaction acts within a single conversation; it doesn't carry across sessions.
Context editing deletes content; it doesn't persist anything.
Correct. Persistence across sessions.
Caching is a cost/latency optimization and it expires; it isn't business memory.

questoes.pergunta: A code migration agent runs long tasks. With a low max_tokens to contain cost, it frequently ends with stop_reason max_tokens in the middle of a half-edited file. The team wants to limit spending but have the agent finish in an orderly way. What should they use?
opcoes: Lower max_tokens even further
A task budget (a visible ceiling: the model plans and wraps up the work), keeping max_tokens as a per-response ceiling
A fixed limit of 5 loop iterations as the main stopping mechanism, combined with an even lower max_tokens per response
Add "be concise" to the prompt
questoes.explicacao: max_tokens is invisible and cuts off midway. A task budget is visible: the model organizes itself to fit.
feedbacks: Truncates even earlier.
Correct. A visible ceiling allows a graceful finish.
An iteration limit as the main stopping mechanism is an anti-pattern; it only serves as a backstop.
A vague instruction doesn't give the model any sense of the ceiling.

questoes.pergunta: A CI job calls the Messages API to review PRs. The code only checks whether the HTTP status is 2xx and then posts content as a comment. On some PRs the job goes green, but the comment comes out empty or with a generic sentence. What is missing?
opcoes: Retry with exponential backoff on 5xx and 429 errors, since empty responses usually indicate API instability
Increase the HTTP client timeout
Switch to the Batch API
Check stop_reason before reading content and handle refusal (HTTP 200) and max_tokens
questoes.explicacao: A refusal arrives with HTTP 200 and stop_reason refusal; truncation, with max_tokens. Code that only looks at the status treats both as success.
feedbacks: There is no 5xx: the response is 200.
There is no timeout; the response arrived.
Batch isn't for a blocking CI step and doesn't solve the detection.
Correct. stop_reason decides.

questoes.pergunta: A support agent has a 12,000-token system prompt with fixed policies and cache_control at the end. To "provide temporal context", the first line of the system prompt is "Current date and time: <ISO 8601 with seconds>". Input cost went up after enabling the cache. What is the fix?
opcoes: Move the date/time to after the last breakpoint (e.g., into the user message)
Change the cache TTL to 1 hour, so the entry survives between requests and is read more often
Add a second breakpoint in the middle of the system prompt
Disable the cache, which doesn't work for large system prompts
questoes.explicacao: A timestamp in the prefix changes on every request: each call pays the cache write (premium) and never reads. Volatile content goes after the last breakpoint.
feedbacks: Correct. Stable first, volatile after.
TTL doesn't help: the prefix changes on every request.
The timestamp is at the beginning; any breakpoint after it is invalidated too.
Caching works well for a large system prompt; the problem is the variable byte.

questoes.pergunta: A platform builds each request's tool list according to the user's profile (sometimes 6, sometimes 9 tools, in different orders). The system prompt has 15,000 tokens and cache_control, but cache_read_input_tokens is almost always 0. What is the cause and the fix?
opcoes: The 15,000-token system prompt is too large for a single cached block; split it into 4 breakpoints of similar size
The 5-minute TTL is short; use 1 hour
Tools come before the system prompt in the prefix; fix the set and order of the tools (or use tool search with defer_loading)
The model doesn't support caching with tools
questoes.explicacao: Prefix order: tools → system → messages. A variable tool list is a silent invalidator. Tool search exists partly so you don't have to modify the tools array.
feedbacks: Breakpoints don't fix a prefix that changes at the beginning.
TTL doesn't help when the prefix changes.
Correct.
Caching works with tools; they are part of the prefix.

questoes.pergunta: After reorganizing the prompt to use caching, how should the team VERIFY, in production, that the cache is being used?
opcoes: Measure average latency before and after and assume the cache is working if it drops consistently
Monitor usage.cache_read_input_tokens; zero on repeated requests indicates invalidation
Check whether the API returned a cache warning in the header
Count how many blocks have cache_control
questoes.explicacao: usage.cache_read_input_tokens shows how much was read from the cache; cache_creation_input_tokens shows how much was written.
feedbacks: Latency is indicative but noisy, and it doesn't prove cache reads.
Correct.
Invalidation and a prefix below the minimum are silent; there is no warning.
Having markers doesn't mean the cache is being read.

questoes.pergunta: A structured extraction team put cache_control on a short system prompt (about 250 tokens) that is repeated across thousands of requests. In the logs, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are always 0, with no error. What is the most likely explanation?
opcoes: There is a hidden timestamp in the system prompt
The cache_control was placed on a block that the API doesn't accept as a breakpoint, and the marker was ignored without an error
The requests go to different regions
The prefix is below the model's minimum cacheable length; in that case there is no caching, silently
questoes.explicacao: Below the minimum cacheable length (which depends on the model), nothing is written or read, and there is no error.
feedbacks: A timestamp would cause a write on every request (creation > 0), not zero.
It's unlikely the API would ignore a valid marker; and the "zero writes" symptom points to size.
That isn't the explanation for writes always being zero.
Correct. Zero creation with a marker = prefix too small.

questoes.pergunta: A productivity assistant answers questions about a 60,000-token technical manual that changes once a month. Each request has: definitions for 4 fixed tools, fixed instructions, the manual, the logged-in user's name, and the question. Which layout makes the best use of the cache?
opcoes: tools → instructions → manual (breakpoint here) → user name and question
tools → user name → instructions → manual → question (breakpoint at the end)
question → manual → instructions → tools, with a breakpoint at the beginning
Cache only the question, which is what changes
questoes.explicacao: Stable first, volatile after: everything that repeats across requests goes before the breakpoint; user data and the question come after.
feedbacks: Correct.
The user's name in the middle of the prefix invalidates the cached manual for each different user; a breakpoint at the end includes the question, which always changes.
The prefix order is tools → system → messages, and volatile content at the beginning invalidates everything.
Caching what changes on every request just pays the write premium.

questoes.pergunta: A team is investigating why an agent's cache is almost never read. Which TWO practices found in the code are silent prompt caching invalidators? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The system prompt is generated by serializing a Dictionary<string, object> without stable key ordering
The user's question comes after the last breakpoint
The breakpoint is on the last block of the stable system prompt
The session ID is inserted into the first line of the system prompt for traceability
The TTL used is the default 5 minutes and there are requests every 30 seconds
questoes.explicacao: Nondeterministic key order changes the prefix bytes; a session ID in the prefix makes each session a distinct prefix.
feedbacks: Correct. Different bytes in the prefix on each serialization.
That is the correct design (volatile content after the breakpoint).
That is also the correct design.
Correct. A variable identifier at the beginning of the prefix.
With requests every 30 s, the 5-min cache stays warm (a read refreshes the TTL).

questoes.pergunta: An architect reviews the context management proposal for a long-running research agent. Which TWO statements in the proposal are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The memory tool automatically reduces the context size of the current session
Compaction is the best way to ensure that exact numeric values are preserved
Compaction is appropriate for long-running work that needs to preserve the narrative of what was tried and why
Editing old messages in the history is a safe way to save tokens
Numbers that will be used as tool arguments should be kept in a case facts block, outside what gets summarized
questoes.explicacao: Compaction preserves narrative (not precision); case facts preserve exact values. The memory tool persists across sessions; editing the history breaks thinking and the cache.
feedbacks: The memory tool persists findings outside the conversation, but it doesn't trim the current context on its own.
Summarization is precisely where numbers get lost.
Correct.
History should be append-only; editing it breaks preserved thinking and invalidates the cache.
Correct.
